              BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA


          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION                      )
          OF OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC                          )
          COMPANY FOR AN ORDER OF THE                           )
          COMMISSION APPROVING NEW EXTRA                        )
          LARGE LOAD TARIFF AND TERMS AND                       )        CASE NO. PUD 2026-000046
          CONDITIONS OF SERVICE FOR EXTRA                       )
          LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS AND A                            )
          REGULATORY ASSET TO RECOVER                           )
          COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH PORTFOLIO                       )
          OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE


             GOOGLE’S PARTIAL AND SUPPLEMENTAL BRIEF IN CHIEF REGARDING
                     ALTERNATIVE ELECTRIC SERVICE FRAMEWORKS

                Google LLC (“Google”) respectfully submit this Partial and Supplemental Brief in Chief

         pursuant to Order No. 761449, issued October 21, 2026, by the Oklahoma Corporation

         Commission (“Commission”) in the above-captioned proceeding concerning Oklahoma Gas and

         Electric Company's (“OG&E”) proposed Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) Tariff.

         Google’s position differed on certain portions of the Joint Brief in Chief (“Joint Brief”) filed by

         Google LLC (“Google”), The Public Utility Division (“PUD”) of the Oklahoma Corporation

         Commission (“Commission”), The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”), Oklahoma

         Sustainability Network (“OSN”), American Association of Retired Persons (“AARP”), and

         Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”) and those portions are listed here as a

         supplement.

                This Partial and Supplemental Brief starts at Section VII of the Joint Brief.




                                                          1
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 18




         VII. HOUSE BILL 2992 SUPPORTS THE COMMISSION'S CONTINUED AUTHORITY
         TO DEVELOP APPROPRIATE LARGE LOAD SERVICE FRAMEWORKS (ITEMS (g),
                                        (h), AND (n))

                    A. HB 2992 establishes customer protections and Commission oversight; it does not
                    prohibit self-supply.

                    House Bill 2992, the Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026, establishes

         a statutory framework for electric service to qualifying large load customers.1The legislation

         requires separate tariffs and terms and conditions of service for qualifying customers, establishes

         minimum contractual commitments, and directs attention to the costs and risks associated with

         serving exceptionally large electric loads. The statute reflects the Legislature's recognition that

         large load customers may present materially different service requirements from those associated

         with traditional customer classes. Such customers may require substantial generation capacity,

         transmission investment, and other infrastructure. They may also create unique risks associated

         with changes in projected load, early departure, or failure to satisfy contractual commitments.

                    HB 2992 responds to those circumstances by establishing statutory protections and

         preserving regulatory oversight. The statute does not, however, expressly prohibit self-supply or

         BYONG arrangements. HB 2992 also does not expressly require every qualifying large load

         customer to purchase all generation supply from the incumbent utility's existing generation

         portfolio.

                    HB 2992 does not independently create the Commission's authority to approve self-supply.

         The Commission's general authority to establish retail rates and conditions of service predates HB

         2992. However, HB 2992 certainly does not withdraw or limit that authority in a manner that

         prohibits the Commission from considering alternative generation procurement arrangements,

         such as self-supply or BYONG. Nothing in the statute establishes such a categorical limitation.


         1
             17 O.S. §§ 900-906.


                                                           2
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 18




         HB 2992 presumes Commission ratemaking for large loads and establishes requirements

         governing the exercise of that authority. It does not freeze tariff design in the form preferred by

         any particular utility.

                 The Commission remains responsible for determining whether a proposed tariff complies

         with the statute, Commission rules, protects existing customers, and establishes appropriate terms

         for the services rendered.

                  B. The Legislature's emphasis on cost causation is consistent with appropriately
                 structured self-supply arrangements.

                 A central purpose of HB 2992 is protecting existing customers from costs attributable to

         serving qualifying large load customers. That objective is consistent with the Commission's

         consideration of appropriately structured self-supply arrangements.

                 When a large load customer self-supplies its load with SPP-accredited capacity and the

         required planning reserve margin, it eliminates the incumbent utility’s generation supply

         obligation for that self-supplied load and the generation capacity costs the utility would otherwise

         incur to serve it.

                 At the same time, the customer continues to use the incumbent utility's transmission,

         delivery, metering, and administrative systems, and a properly designed tariff assigns the customer

         the costs of the utility delivery infrastructure and services it actually uses in accordance with cost

         causation.

                 HB 2992 establishes guardrails for large load service. It does not compel the Commission

         to reject potentially lawful generation procurement arrangements before evaluating their actual

         costs and regulatory consequences.

                 C. The absence of a self-supply authorization does not establish an implied
                 prohibition.




                                                           3
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 18




                Oklahoma statutes must be interpreted according to their text. Assertions concerning

         proposals discussed during legislative negotiations cannot substitute for enacted statutory

         requirements. If the Legislature intended to prohibit all self-supply or BYONG arrangements by

         qualifying large load customers, it would have stated that prohibition expressly. It did not. Other

         statutory provisions, including RESCTA, must still be satisfied. But HB 2992's omission cannot

         itself establish a categorical restriction that eliminates the Commission's otherwise existing

         authority. Unenacted proposals are unreliable guides to legislative intent even when documented,

         and undocumented accounts of private legislative negotiations are entitled to no weight. The

         argument also cuts both ways: if HB 2992’s silence does not authorize self-supply, neither does it

         prohibit a framework otherwise within the Commission’s constitutional ratemaking authority. The

         relevant silence is the absence of any prohibition.

                D. Section 903 requires a separate tariff for the large load class defined in Section
                901(4) without further subdivision, and does not prohibit a self-supply election within
                that tariff (Item (g)).

                Read together, 17 O.S. §§ 901(4) and 903 require an electric supplier to establish a separate

         tariff applicable to qualifying new large load customers (new data centers, cryptocurrency mining

         operations, and artificial-intelligence computing facilities contracting to add 75 MW or greater

         behind a single point of interconnection after July 1, 2026) as a defined class, rather than requiring

         separate tariffs subdivided by specific computational end use. Nothing in Section 901(4) or Section

         903 prohibits that large load tariff from including a customer self-supply election.

                E. A Customer Class Protection Charge that is not grounded in cost of service violates
                the cost-causation mandate of 17 O.S. § 902 (Item (h)).

                Section 902 of HB 2992 requires the Commission to ensure that all rates are fair, just, and

         reasonable, and that costs and revenues are assigned and allocated among customers in accordance

         with cost causation principles. Section 903 similarly requires that large load tariffs ensure that


                                                           4
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 18




         customers reimburse the electric supplier for the costs fairly allocated to them under Section 902.

         Under both HB 2992 and the Commission's constitutional ratemaking authority under Article IX,

         Section 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution and 17 O.S. § 152, every customer must pay the

         demonstrated costs of the utility system and services it uses, but may not be assessed arbitrary,

         non-cost-based surcharges unrelated to the cost of serving its load.

                Accordingly, a Customer Class Protection Charge (or any relabeled surcharge not

         grounded in demonstrated cost of service) that recovers no cost incurred to serve large load

         customers and operates as an additional exaction on top of full cost-of-service recovery violates

         the plain text of 17 O.S. §§ 902 and 903. In its rebuttal testimony, OG&E itself conceded that it

         does not present its proposed Customer Class Protection Charge as recovery of a cost incurred to

         serve XLPL customers and that the charge operates on top of full cost recovery. Because cost

         causation requires that a customer pay the costs of the system it uses rather than unincurred or

         arbitrary charges, a non-cost-based Customer Class Protection Charge violates Section 902.

           VIII. THE COMMISSION MAY CONSIDER ALTERNATIVE ELECTRIC SERVICE
                 FRAMEWORKS WITHOUT AUTHORIZING RETAIL WHEELING OR
                             DEREGULATION (ITEMS (c) AND (d))

                OG&E's rebuttal testimony characterizes the proposals advanced by intervenors as

         mechanisms for obtaining generation outside the utility's bundled service framework. That

         characterization does not establish that the proposals authorize retail wheeling or retail electric

         competition.

                Under 17 O.S. § 190.3(8), retail wheeling means the transmission or distribution facilities

         of an electric utility being used to transport electric energy from a competing retail electric supplier

         to a retail electric consumer, with the third party making a retail sale and the utility acting only as

         a transporter for a fee. The definition matters, because a jurisdictional holding should not rest on




                                                            5
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 18




         a formulation a party has written for the occasion. A self-supply or BYONG option involves no

         retail sale by a third party and no transportation service rendered by the incumbent on any third

         party’s behalf to a retail customer. A properly designed option requires that all self-supply be

         coordinated with the incumbent and that all retail electric service be supplied through the

         incumbent. The third-party seller delivers into the SPP market at its settlement location; the

         incumbent, as the load-responsible entity, serves its retail customer’s entire load from the market

         and its own resources and bills the customer under its own tariff.

                    The contention that the incumbent is merely wheeling because it is “not generating” the

         energy its customer consumes substitutes a different test for the statutory one. A retail electric

         supplier does not cease to be the retail electric supplier because a portion of the energy its customer

         consumes was procured under a contract the supplier did not sign. Every utility in SPP serves its

         load in part with energy purchased in the Integrated Marketplace from generators it does not own;

         none of them is thereby wheeling to its own customers.

                    The retail wheeling objection also confronts a difficulty its proponents do not address. To

         the extent opponents insist that the self-supplied energy involves a wholesale sale and associated

         transmission service, those matters lie within FERC’s exclusive jurisdiction, and a state may not

         recharacterize them as retail.2 The objection is therefore either wrong on the facts or preempted on

         the law.

                    Nor does a self-supply option introduce retail competition. Oklahoma has not opened retail

         electric supply to competition. The Electric Restructuring Act of 1997 established a framework for

         studying a transition to customer choice, but its implementation was not carried forward, and

         Oklahoma retail customers today take service from the certificated supplier for their territory. The



         2
             16 U.S.C. §§ 824(b)(1), 824(d); Nantahala, 476 U.S. at 966; Miss. Power & Light, 487 U.S. at 371–72.


                                                                   6
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 18




         Joint Parties do not contend otherwise, and a self-supply option does not depend on any

         restructuring authority. Retail competition means that a customer may choose among competing

         retail suppliers, each of which sells and bills retail electric service to the customer, with the

         incumbent’s wires used to deliver a competitor’s retail product. A self-supply option does none of

         that. The customer has one retail supplier, the incumbent, and what the customer procures from

         others is SPP-accredited wholesale capacity and energy in a federally regulated market.

                 Nor does 17 O.S. § 190.3(9) impliedly prohibit self-supply for customers of jurisdictional

         utilities. That subsection defines “retail electric service distributor” and permits municipal utilities,

         their beneficial trusts, and the Grand River Dam Authority (entities otherwise outside the

         Commission’s rate jurisdiction) to opt into the statutory scheme by rendering service on an open

         access basis. The subject of the provision is the jurisdictional status of non-jurisdictional entities.

         It does not address the terms on which a jurisdictional utility may serve a customer that owns or

         contracts for generation. The canon expressio unius est exclusio alterius is an aid used to determine

         legislative intent, not a rule that manufactures prohibitions from silence. It operates on parallel

         items within a common statutory subject; it does not permit the Commission to infer, from a

         definition governing municipal opt-in to open access, a prohibition on customer self-supply that

         appears nowhere in the Oklahoma Statutes.

                 Finally, the warning that a self-supply option would make Oklahoma the first state in SPP

         to move toward retail competition outruns the proposal. A self-supply option applies to a narrowly

         defined class of very large customers, opens no customer class to competitive retail supply, and

         permits no other entity to furnish retail electric service.

                 The Commission should therefore reject the proposition that every customer-supported

         wholesale generation arrangement constitutes retail wheeling or unlawful deregulation.




                                                            7
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 18




               IX. UTILITY GENERATION OBLIGATIONS UNDER SELF-SUPPLY AND
             LIMITATIONS ON PRE-SERVICE MONTHLY CHARGES (ITEMS (f) AND (i))

                A. Customer self-supply eliminates the incumbent utility's obligation to build,
                procure, or hold generation capacity for self-supplied load, and a certificate under
                RESCTA confers no right to compel customers to purchase utility generation (Item
                (f)).

                 Under Oklahoma law (17 O.S. §§ 152, 158.25), a regulated utility's service obligations are

         defined and bounded by the terms of its Commission-approved tariffs and the specific retail

         services a customer elects to take. When a large load customer elects to self-supply its generation

         requirements by providing SPP-accredited capacity sufficient to cover 100 percent of its peak load

         plus the applicable SPP Planning Reserve Margin, that election eliminates any obligation on the

         part of the incumbent utility to build, procure, or hold generation capacity for the self-supplied

         load. Because the customer satisfies the SPP resource adequacy requirement directly through its

         own accredited capacity and reserve margin, the incumbent utility's obligation is limited strictly to

         providing the retail transmission, delivery, metering, and billing services the customer actually

         takes and pays for under the tariff.

                 Nor does a certificated utility hold any statutory entitlement to force a customer to purchase

         utility-owned generation capacity that the customer does not use. A certificate of authority under

         RESCTA (17 O.S. § 158.25) grants an exclusive right against competing retail electric suppliers

         within the utility's certified territory; it does not confer a monopoly right to construct utility rate-

         base generation for load that a customer self-supplies with accredited capacity in SPP.

                 B. The Commission lacks statutory authority to impose a monthly service charge
                 where no electric service is provided, while post-energization cost recovery is
                 governed by the tariff's contractual minimum bill structure (Item (i)).

                 Under Article IX, Section 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution and 17 O.S. §§ 151, 152, 284,

         and 902, utility rates must be grounded in cost causation and compensate a utility only for electric




                                                            8
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 18




         service rendered using facilities that are used and useful in serving the public. In circumstances

         where no electric service is provided, such as prior to commercial operation when a customer's

         facility is not energized and no utility facilities are in commercial service for the customer,

         assessing a recurring monthly service charge (such as OG&E's proposed pre-service reservation

         charge) violates cost causation and exceeds the Commission's statutory ratemaking authority.

         Legitimate pre-commercial engineering and early procurement costs incurred prior to energization

         are already recovered through direct cost advances under a preliminary engineering agreement.

                Once retail service commences under the Electric Service Agreement, electric service is

         being provided, and the large load tariff's contractual minimum bill and take-or-pay structure

         obligates the customer to pay the prudently incurred transmission and delivery costs caused to

         serve that customer.

           X. FUNCTIONAL RATE UNBUNDLING, COST-BASED SELF-SUPPLY CHARGES,
            AND CAPACITY CREDITING FULLY COMPLY WITH OKLAHOMA LAW AND
                                  COST CAUSATION

                A. Functional unbundling of generation and transmission rates is necessary to
                implement self-supply, is prohibited by no Oklahoma statute or rule, and is squarely
                within the Commission's rate design authority

                Implementing a self-supply option requires functional rate unbundling on the large load

         tariff schedule (separately stating the functional generation demand charge and the functional

         transmission and delivery demand charge) so that a self-supplying customer pays the delivery rates

         for the transmission and delivery system it uses and does not pay embedded generation charges

         for utility generation capacity it does not use.

                As to Item (j), there is no legal barrier, statute, or Commission rule in Oklahoma that

         prohibits OG&E from unbundling and separately stating functional generation and transmission

         rate components on a retail tariff schedule for rate design transparency. Neither the Oklahoma




                                                            9
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 18




         Constitution, Title 17 of the Oklahoma Statutes (including RESCTA, 17 O.S. §§ 158.21 et seq.,

         the Electric Restructuring Act, 17 O.S. §§ 190.1 et seq., and HB 2992, 17 O.S. §§ 901-905), nor

         Title 165 of the Oklahoma Administrative Code requires generation and transmission charges to

         be combined into a single bundled rate. On the contrary, the Commission's Minimum Standard

         Filing Requirements (OAC 165:70-5-4, Section L Class Cost of Service Study) already require

         regulated utilities in every general rate case to functionalize, classify, and allocate their revenue

         requirement separately across production demand, production energy, transmission demand, and

         distribution functions. Separately stating those functionalized generation and transmission charges

         on the face of a retail tariff schedule does not unbundle retail transmission into a standalone service

         under FERC Order No. 888 or authorize retail wheeling, because the customer continues to take

         retail electric service exclusively from the incumbent utility under a state-regulated tariff.

                  The Commission has clear constitutional and statutory authority under Article IX, Section

         18 of the Oklahoma Constitution, 17 O.S. §§ 152 and 153, and 17 O.S. §§ 902 and 903 to request

         or direct OG&E to unbundle and separately state functional generation and transmission rate

         components in a retail tariff. The Commission's plenary authority to fix and establish just and

         reasonable rates in accordance with cost causation includes the authority to require transparent,

         functionalized rate schedules derived directly from Section L of the utility's Class Cost of Service

         Study.

                  B. It is just, reasonable, and in the public interest for every customer to pay its share
                  of the system costs it uses, and a customer that self-supplies accredited capacity plus
                  the reserve margin imposes no generation capacity costs on OG&E's system.

                  Item (l) asks whether it is just, reasonable, and in the public interest for a self-supplying

         customer to pay no generation demand charges or related costs to OG&E when self-supplying.

         Under the cost-causation mandate of 17 O.S. § 902 and Article IX, Section 18 of the Oklahoma




                                                           10
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 18




         Constitution, it is just, reasonable, and in the public interest for every customer to pay its share of

         the costs of the utility system it uses, and not to be charged for utility services it does not use or

         arbitrary costs it does not cause.

                When a self-supplying customer brings its own SPP-accredited, deliverable generation

         capacity sufficient to cover 100 percent of its peak demand plus the applicable SPP Planning

         Reserve Margin, that customer is not imposing any additional generation capacity costs on

         OG&E's system. Embedded utility generation demand charges exist to recover the fixed capital

         and operating costs of the utility's generation fleet built or procured to serve customers taking

         utility generation supply. Because OG&E does not build, procure, or hold generation capacity for

         load that is covered by customer-supplied accredited capacity and reserve margin, the self-

         supplying customer's cost-causation share of OG&E's generation demand charge for that load is

         zero. Requiring a self-supplying customer to pay OG&E's generation demand charges on top of

         financing its own accredited generation capacity and reserve margin would force the customer to

         pay twice for generation and violate 17 O.S. § 902.

                At the same time, a self-supplying customer always pays the cost of the utility system it

         actually uses. The customer uses OG&E's transmission, delivery, metering, and administrative

         systems, and pays 100 percent of its allocated share of those costs, including upfront Contributions

         in Aid of Construction for dedicated interconnection facilities, unbundled transmission and

         substation delivery demand charges, base non-fuel delivery charges, and applicable transmission

         riders. Nor does this result shift costs onto existing ratepayers: OG&E's existing generation fleet

         was built for and is used by existing customers, whose generation costs do not increase when a

         new customer brings its own accredited capacity while contributing new revenues toward shared

         transmission and delivery infrastructure. Ensuring that a self-supplying customer pays in full for




                                                           11
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 18




         the delivery system it uses, while paying zero for utility generation capacity it does not use or

         cause the utility to incur, is the exact definition of just, reasonable, and cost-based ratemaking in

         the public interest.

                 Finally, while a customer that supplies 100 percent of its SPP-accredited capacity and

         required reserve margin should not cause OG&E to incur generation-related costs for that self-

         supplied load, the ultimate determination of what costs are attributable to a self-supplying

         customer is an evidentiary question for the Commission under 17 O.S. § 902. If the Commission

         determines from the evidentiary record that OG&E actually incurs any specific, quantifiable

         generation-related costs attributable to serving a self-supplying customer, cost causation requires

         that those demonstrated costs be included on the self-supplying customer's bill and paid by that

         customer. A self-supplying customer does not seek to avoid any demonstrated cost it causes on the

         system; if the evidentiary record establishes that such costs exist, the customer will pay them. That

         factual question of whether any such costs are demonstrated in the record goes to the specific rate

         design of the tariff, not to the Commission's threshold legal authority to approve a self-supply

         framework.

                 C. Legal and operational considerations for implementing bilateral consideration of
                 credited capacity supply (Item (m)).

                 Should the Commission find that Oklahoma's ratepayers and economy benefit from

         encouraging appropriate self-supply, bilateral consideration of customer-supplied capacity should

         be implemented through clear, objective rules grounded in cost causation (17 O.S. §§ 902-903)

         and SPP tariff requirements so that the customer pays for the system it uses without shifting

         generation costs or risks onto existing ratepayers:

                 1. SPP Capacity Accreditation and Planning Reserve Margin. Customer-supplied

         capacity must be credited at its seasonal Accredited Capacity value under applicable SPP resource


                                                          12
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 18




         adequacy rules (such as Effective Load Carrying Capability or Performance-Based Accreditation,

         rather than nameplate capacity) in an amount sufficient to cover 100 percent of the customer's self-

         supplied peak demand plus the full applicable SPP Planning Reserve Margin.

                2. SPP Deliverability. Qualifying generation resources must be located within the SPP

         footprint and hold firm transmission deliverability or Network Integration Transmission Service

         designation under the SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff.

                3. SPP Registration and Load-Responsible Entity Attribution. Because the incumbent

         utility serves as the Load Responsible Entity for retail load in its settlement area, customer-

         supplied capacity must be properly registered and attributed through applicable SPP tariff

         mechanisms (such as SPP Market Participant and Attachment AM Meter Agent arrangements or

         a utility pass-through sleeve) so that the capacity counts directly toward the SPP resource adequacy

         obligation for the customer's load without double counting.

                4. Direct Functional Rate Offset Without Cross-Class Subsidies. Crediting of qualified

         customer-supplied capacity must operate directly between the customer and the utility by setting

         the unbundled utility generation charge to zero for the self-supplied load, rather than paying

         monetary bill credits recovered from existing ratepayers through the Fuel Adjustment Clause or

         base rates. Any SPP capacity deficiency penalties or market replacement costs caused by a shortfall

         in the customer's supplied capacity must be assigned directly to the self-supplying customer.

                5. Full Recovery of Delivery System Costs and Resource Neutrality. The self-supplying

         customer must pay in full for the utility delivery infrastructure and services it uses (including

         upfront Contributions in Aid of Construction for dedicated interconnection facilities and

         unbundled transmission and delivery rates), and the framework must remain technology- and fuel-

         neutral for any resource meeting SPP accreditation and deliverability standards.




                                                         13
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 18




              XI. OTHER LEGAL ISSUES NECESSARY TO EVALUATE THE POSITIONS
                                   ADVANCED (ITEM (n))

                 A. The Commission has authority to approve a self-supply tariff framework in this
                 proceeding and direct a compliance filing to populate mechanical rate components
                 from OG&E's Class Cost of Service Study.

                 Under Article IX, Section 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution and 17 O.S. § 152, the

         Commission routinely approves tariff structures and rate design principles in a final order and

         directs the utility to submit conforming compliance tariff sheets populated from its approved Class

         Cost of Service Study. Opponents cannot contend that a self-supply framework is beyond the

         Commission's legal authority merely because mechanical functional rate calculations from the

         utility's existing Section L cost-of-service records follow in a compliance filing subject to

         Commission review.

                 B. Comparisons to other jurisdictions establish no legal barrier under Oklahoma law.

                 That a different commission, applying a different statute, in a different regional

         transmission organization, approved a large load tariff without a self-supply option is not evidence

         that a self-supply option is unlawful in Oklahoma. No party contends that another state's law

         governs here, and HB 2992 does not require the Commission to replicate another state's tariff

         structure.

         XII. THE COMMISSION SHOULD RECOGNIZE ITS AUTHORITY TO CONSIDER
         APPROPRIATELY STRUCTURED SELF-SUPPLY ARRANGEMENTS WHILE
         RESERVING DETERMINATIONS REGARDING PARTICULAR PROPOSALS

                 Order No. 761449 established supplemental briefing to address substantial legal and

         jurisdictional issues concerning alternative electric service frameworks. Those issues are

         appropriately resolved by distinguishing the Commission's existing authority from the merits of

         any particular proposal.




                                                         14
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 18




                 The Commission possesses constitutional and statutory authority to establish the rates and

         conditions under which regulated electric utilities furnish retail service. RESCTA protects the

         exclusivity of certificated retail service territories but does not categorically prohibit wholesale

         generation transactions associated with a retail customer's load. The Federal Power Act recognizes

         the jurisdictional distinction between wholesale transactions and retail service. HB 2992

         establishes protections governing service to qualifying large load customers without expressly

         prohibiting appropriately structured wholesale generation procurement arrangements, such as self-

         supply or BYONG.

                 Together, these authorities establish that the Commission may consider a retail tariff

         accommodating self-supply or BYONG where the incumbent utility remains the certificated retail

         electric supplier and the arrangement otherwise complies with applicable law.

                 This conclusion does not authorize a competing retail supplier to furnish service within

         another utility's certified territory, nor does it relieve a large load customer of responsibility for the

         delivery system costs it causes. It simply recognizes that the Commission's existing ratemaking

         authority encompasses retail service arrangements that distinguish between generation supply

         procured by a customer in SPP and the retail delivery services furnished by the incumbent utility.

                 The Commission should therefore reject any categorical interpretation of Oklahoma law

         under which a self-supply or BYONG arrangement constitutes unauthorized retail wheeling,

         unlawful restructuring, or a violation of RESCTA.

                                                 XIII. CONCLUSION

                 For the foregoing reasons, Google submits this Partial and Supplemental Brief in Chief and

         respectfully request that the Commission recognize and determine that:




                                                            15
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 111 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 16 OF 18




                 1. The Commission possesses constitutional and statutory authority to consider and

         approve retail electric service tariffs and arrangements that accommodate customer self-supply,

         including appropriately structured wholesale generation procurement arrangements.

                 2. RESCTA does not categorically prohibit such arrangements where the incumbent

         certificated utility remains the entity furnishing retail electric service to the consuming facility and

         no competing supplier furnishes unauthorized retail electric service within the incumbent's

         certified territory.

                 3. Wholesale generation transactions conducted pursuant to applicable FERC-

         jurisdictional arrangements, including transactions scheduled and settled through SPP’s Integrated

         Marketplace, do not become retail electric service merely because the energy or economic benefits

         associated with those transactions support a particular retail customer's load.

                 4. HB 2992 does not prohibit the Commission from considering appropriately structured

         self-supply arrangements, provided that the applicable statutory requirements and protections are

         satisfied.

                 5. Functional unbundling of generation-related and transmission-related rate components

         on a retail tariff schedule is not prohibited by Oklahoma statute or rule and lies squarely within the

         Commission's constitutional and statutory rate design authority, and a self-supplying customer that

         provides SPP-accredited capacity plus the required reserve margin should not be charged for utility

         generation capacity it does not use, while remaining responsible to pay its share of the delivery

         system costs it uses and any other specific costs the Commission determines from the evidentiary

         record are attributable to serving that customer.
